newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Bank of Portugal surprises markets with cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bank of Portugal surprises markets with cut.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal cut its key money market rates 0.30 percent on Friday in a show of confidence that inflation is well under control.

The move, which took most analysts by surprise, was seen as a signal that June inflation figures, due to be released by the National Statistics Institute (INE) on Monday, will confirm that inflation is slowing again after quickening in May.
"For me -- and I think for all -- it was a surprise. I think it has to do with the conviction that inflation will renew its downward trend in June," said Isabel Cabral of brokers Fincor.
The Bank, which lowered the key repurchase pact rate to 5.7 percent, had been expected to wait until later in July before moving on interest rates.

May inflation figures jolted the market when they showed prices rising 0.7 percent compared with the previous month and 2.1 percent year-on-year. In April, the year-on-year rate had slowed to just 1.8 percent.
Analysts are forecasting that the monthly rate will show a rise of no more than 0.3 percent in June and could even register a slight fall.

The cut in interest rates was the latest in a series of upbeat developments for the Portuguese economy which is growing far faster than the Socialist government had predicted when it drew up its budget plans for 1997.

On Thursday, the Labour Ministry announced the sharpest year-on-year drop in unemployment for four years. The unemployment rate now stands at some 6.5 percent, down from 7.2 percent at the same point last year.

The quickening economic growth, with the economy widely expected to grow at least 3.5 percent, against the official projection of 3.0 percent, means that Portugal should have little problem in meeting the budget deficit target for entry to the European Union's single currency, analysts say.

"The growth aids revenues as it makes more people pay more taxes and reduces layouts for unemployment and social spending," said Rui Martins dos Santos, chief economist at Banco Portugues do Investimento (BPI).
The government plans to produce a state deficit of 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), just below the three percent limit for economic and monetary union (EMU).
The central bank's rate cut demonstrates that inflation should also not prove a barrier to Portugal's access to the single currency elite, they added.
